newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU launches campaign to promote Euro.
newsitem.headline: German CDU launches campaign to promote Euro.

text.p: Germany's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) launched a campaign for Europe's single currency on Wednesday, a day after economic institutes said Bonn would not meet the Maastricht treaty's 1999 deadline.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's staunchly pro-European party will hold rallies across Germany where politicians and bankers aim to drum up support with the help of a special CD-ROM disk packed with a film, graphics and figures on the new money.

The campaign, titled "A currency for a safer future", will portray the Euro as a trading, investment and reserve currency competing against the dollar and yen and hail the benefits of currency stability within Europe.

"The introduction of the Euro is the most important project for the future of Europe," said CDU party chairman Peter Hinze before a large billboard showing a Euro coin with its stars half-covering the oak leaves on a one-mark coin.

Hintze rejected a suggestion by leading economists on Tuesday that Germany, the leading force behind the drive for a single currency, would not itself meet the tough Maastricht Treaty criteria to limit state debt and deficit spending.
"Germany will fulfil the criteria. The European train will leave on schedule," he told journalists. For worried Germans, he added: "The Euro will be as hard and as strong as the mark."

Germany's six top economic institutes said in their autumn forecast on Tuesday that the 1997 deficit would be 3.5 percent of gross domestic product -- above the Maastricht treaty's three percent goal for joining monetary union planned in 1999.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Bonn would stick to a strict course and "create the conditions so that the 1997 deficit lies below three percent of gross domestic product".
Next year is crucial for deciding which countries will participate in EMU at the scheduled start in January 1999.
Hintze said the CDU campaign would kick off with a rally in Bonn on December 10. Similar meetings would be held in all of Germany's 16 federal states.
He agreed many Germans were sceptical about the Euro but said this stemmed mostly from a lack of knowledge about it.

The Euro debate resurfaced in Germany at the weekend when Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder of the opposition Social Democrat party (SPD) said he thought the government should call off the project now.

Party colleagues rushed to defend the Euro, stressing the SPD support for European monetary union. It is desperate to shake off its anti-European reputation, gained after a regional election campaign in March which backfired.

SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine said on Tuesday the Euro was a tool to fight unemployment in the European Union. He and Schroeder are likely to be the two leading candidates to become the SPD's challenger to Chancellor Helmut Kohl in the 1998 general elections.
